paragraphs: A decision maker may care both about what happens and about how much uncertainty remains. Standard partially observable Markov decision processes describe decisions when the underlying state cannot be observed directly. However, rewards tied to that underlying state cannot express some objectives that explicitly reward reducing uncertainty.

The paper introduces rho-POMDPs, in which rewards depend on the belief state: the decision maker’s current distribution of possibilities about the hidden state. This makes the current state of knowledge part of what an action can improve. An information-seeking objective can therefore be represented directly within the reward function.

The main result assumes that the belief-dependent reward is convex and establishes that the value function is convex too. Under this assumption, the reward can be approximated arbitrarily closely by a piecewise linear, convex function. This structure allows existing exact and approximate POMDP solvers to be adapted with limited changes, connecting the richer objective to established computational methods.
neurips-2010-a-pomdp-extension-with-beli.tldr: Belief-dependent rewards extend POMDPs to uncertainty-reduction objectives while retaining useful convex structure under a convexity assumption.

paragraphs: Inhibitory control is the ability to change or cancel a planned action as new information arrives. The paper treats this ability as a decision problem: an agent must choose what to do while consequences remain uncertain and the demands of the task may change. It applies this perspective to the classical stop-signal task.

The model combines Bayesian inference with stochastic control. Inference addresses uncertainty in the available sensory information, while control determines how to act given that uncertainty. The resulting optimal policy varies systematically with the relative costs of action choices, sensory noise, and the dynamics of changing environmental demands.

This framework accounts for a range of stop-signal behavior observed in humans and animals. Its significance is that stopping behavior can be explained through adaptive decisions that respond to evidence and rewards. The agreement suggests that inhibitory control may involve statistically optimal decision making, but the abstract presents this as an interpretation of behavioral agreement rather than direct proof of the brain’s implementation.
neurips-2010-a-rational-decision-making-.tldr: A Bayesian control model explains inhibitory behavior as adaptive decision making shaped by uncertainty, changing demands, and action costs.

paragraphs: Detecting whether a person is speaking often relies on matching visible movements with an audio signal. This paper investigates a different starting point: movements of facial muscle groups can themselves provide enough information for accurate speech detection. The resulting visual detector works across people and does not require audio to decide whether someone is talking.

The visual detector also supplies information for training audio models associated with particular people. This connects a person-independent visual capability to person-dependent voice recognition. Once trained, the voice model can identify when its person is speaking even if that person is outside the camera’s view, an ability relevant to settings such as mobile robotics.

The authors also combine the visual and auditory models through a simple sensory fusion scheme and report improved talking detection. Experiments on a challenging database support both the visual-only approach and the subsequent use of audio. The findings show how one sensing modality can help train another while their combination provides an additional performance benefit.
neurips-2010-an-alternative-to-low-level.tldr: Facial movements support accurate visual speech detection and can train person-specific voice models that also work when the speaker is unseen.

paragraphs: Matrix completion uses observed entries of a matrix to estimate entries that are missing. In collaborative filtering, the observations need not be distributed evenly across the matrix. This paper examines how that uneven sampling affects a common learning approach based on trace-norm regularization, which constrains the matrix being fitted.

The authors show that non-uniform sampling can substantially damage the performance of ordinary trace-norm regularization. Their proposed response is a properly weighted version of the same regularizer. The central idea is that the sampling pattern matters to how the model should be constrained, rather than being merely a detail of which entries happen to be available.

The paper reports that the weighted approach works well under non-uniform sampling and produces significant gains on the Netflix dataset, where observations are highly uneven. This result connects the methodological change to a collaborative-filtering application. It establishes that adjusting the regularizer can make a meaningful difference in this setting, without claiming that every weighting choice will have the same effect.
neurips-2010-collaborative-filtering-in-.tldr: Properly weighting trace-norm regularization improves matrix completion under uneven sampling, with significant gains reported on Netflix data.

paragraphs: Many discrete optimization problems in machine learning can be expressed as submodular minimization. Submodular functions play a role analogous to convex functions in continuous optimization, and general algorithms have strong polynomial-time guarantees. The practical problem is that those guarantees do not make the available general-purpose methods fast enough for many applications.

The paper identifies a more structured subclass called decomposable submodular functions. These functions can be written as sums in which a concave function is applied to a linear function. The proposed SLG algorithm uses that structure together with results from smoothed convex minimization to handle problems containing tens of thousands of variables.

Experiments cover synthetic benchmarks and a task combining classification with segmentation. On those problems, SLG outperforms general-purpose submodular minimization methods by several orders of magnitude. The contribution is therefore a substantial practical acceleration for the specified decomposable subclass: the additional mathematical structure makes it possible to solve large instances much more efficiently.
neurips-2010-efficient-minimization-of-d.tldr: SLG exploits decomposable submodular structure to solve large problems several orders of magnitude faster than general-purpose methods in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Approximate policy iteration and approximate value iteration repeatedly update estimates used to choose actions. Each update can introduce approximation error or leave a Bellman residual, meaning a discrepancy in the consistency relation the estimates are meant to satisfy. This paper asks how these intermediate errors affect the quality of the final policy.

The analysis quantifies performance loss using Lp measures of the errors at individual iterations. It also changes how a relevant distribution enters the bound: the dependence is through the expected square of a Radon-Nikodym derivative, a mathematical measure of distributional mismatch, rather than its largest value. This replaces a worst-point quantity used in earlier results with an expectation-based quantity.

The results also distinguish when errors occur. Later errors contribute more prominently to performance loss, while the effect of earlier errors decreases exponentially quickly. This gives a more detailed account of error propagation than treating all iterations alike, showing why the accuracy of later updates has particular importance within the analysis.
neurips-2010-error-propagation-for-appro.tldr: The analysis bounds policy loss from iterative approximation errors and shows that earlier errors lose influence exponentially quickly.

paragraphs: Some data require models that represent local relationships while allowing extreme observations to be part of the distribution. Cumulative distribution networks address this by multiplying cumulative distribution functions to build multivariate models, including heavy-tailed ones. Their inference and learning calculations involve mixed derivatives, and existing exact methods were restricted to tree-shaped graphs.

The paper develops an algorithm for computing these derivatives on graphs of arbitrary topology, including graphs with cycles. It recursively divides the calculation into smaller pieces organized through junction trees. This decomposition exploits the model’s sparse structure, addressing a weakness of general symbolic differentiation programs that do not use that structure.

The authors compare the algorithm with Mathematica and D* and apply it to rainfall and H1N1 data. In those applications, networks containing cycles fit the data significantly better than tree-structured and unstructured networks, as well as the compared copula and logistic models. The result connects expanded exact computation to a practical benefit from representing richer dependence patterns.
neurips-2010-exact-inference-and-learnin.tldr: A junction-tree derivative algorithm enables exact computation in cyclic cumulative distribution networks, which achieve better fits in the reported applications.

paragraphs: Mixture models represent data using multiple components, and expectation maximization is a widely used way to fit them. Its expectation step becomes expensive because its work grows linearly with both the number of observations and the number of components. This creates a bottleneck when either part of the model is large.

The paper proposes an alternative within the variational expectation-maximization framework. It organizes observations into partitions that are specific to individual mixture components. Using this structure, the method obtains an expectation step whose cost is sub-linear in sample size while retaining a proof of convergence.

The authors report that the approach is significantly faster than the previous work it builds on and scales better as the number of components increases. Experiments on large synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the speedup. The contribution brings together two properties that matter for large-scale fitting: reducing the dominant computation and preserving a formal convergence guarantee for the resulting algorithm.
neurips-2010-fast-large-scale-mixture-mo.tldr: Component-specific data partitions make the mixture-model expectation step sub-linear in sample size while preserving provable convergence.

paragraphs: A model can perform well at denoising or filling missing image regions without generating convincing images itself. This paper focuses on the more direct test of drawing samples and examining whether they resemble natural images. It investigates why existing models produce high-resolution samples whose shortcomings are apparent even through visual inspection.

The proposed modification introduces two sets of hidden variables. One models pixel intensities, while the other models the image-specific covariances that describe how pixels vary together. The resulting model can be understood as a gated Markov random field: hidden-variable states modulate both average pixel intensities and pairwise pixel dependencies.

With this augmentation, the authors report substantially more realistic high-resolution samples. They also examine how parameters are shared across overlapping receptive fields. Disallowing that weight sharing produces more efficient internal representations, as demonstrated on several recognition tasks. The findings concern both the appearance of generated images and the usefulness of the representations learned within the model.
neurips-2010-generating-more-realistic-i.tldr: Separate latent variables for pixel intensities and image-specific covariances produce more realistic high-resolution image samples.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether unusual long-term physiological activity can help identify cardiac patients at elevated risk. Its central measure, symbolic mismatch, compares long electrocardiographic recordings without relying on specialized medical knowledge. The underlying hypothesis is that high-risk individuals may stand out through differences in their activity patterns.

The method converts ECG signals into symbolic representations and quantifies differences between pairs of those representations. The authors then use this measure with a one-class support vector machine, a nearest-neighbor classifier, and hierarchical clustering. These provide different ways to turn similarities and differences across patients into risk stratification.

Evaluation involved 686 cardiac patients with long-term ECG data. In univariate analyses, all three methods had statistically significant associations with major adverse cardiac events over the next 90 days. After incorporating widely used clinical risk variables, the nearest-neighbor and clustering approaches significantly distinguished patients with roughly twice the risk. These findings support the risk-stratification value of the signal patterns; they concern observed risk associations rather than demonstrated benefits from changing treatment.
neurips-2010-identifying-patients-at-ris.tldr: Symbolic comparisons of long-term ECG signals identified groups with elevated 90-day cardiac-event risk in a study of 686 patients.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model may require understanding how its inferred marginal probabilities change when model parameters change. If a loss is defined on those marginals, training needs derivatives that connect the inference results back to the parameters. This paper presents a finite-difference method for obtaining that information in discrete graphical models.

The key procedure runs inference twice with slightly perturbed parameters. The resulting inference calculations provide the information needed to differentiate an arbitrary loss defined on the marginals. This makes repeated use of the inference procedure itself the central computational device for implicit differentiation.

The method also applies when inference is approximate, with the loss then defined over the approximate marginals. With suitable loss choices, the authors describe practical fitting for models with hidden variables, high treewidth, or model misspecification. The contribution is a simple route from marginal-based objectives to parameter derivatives, including settings where the inference outputs used for learning are themselves approximations.
neurips-2010-implicit-differentiation-by.tldr: Two inference runs at slightly perturbed parameters support finite-difference differentiation of losses defined on graphical-model marginals.

paragraphs: The sequence memoizer is a model for sequential data with strong established performance in language modeling and compression. This paper improves both the model and the procedures used to perform inference with it. Its focus is on making an already effective approach more flexible, more memory-efficient, and more clearly grounded mathematically.

The proposed changes enlarge the range of available hyperparameters and introduce a representation that uses memory more efficiently. The authors also develop inference algorithms that operate on this new representation. These changes address linked aspects of the method: what model settings can be expressed, how the model is stored, and how calculations are performed.

The derivations begin with precise definitions of the underlying processes. Those definitions also support an elementary proof of the coagulation and fragmentation properties used in the original sequence memoizer. Experimental results provide support for the proposed improvements. The paper therefore contributes both practical modifications and a clearer explanation of mathematical properties on which the model depends.
neurips-2010-improvements-to-the-sequenc.tldr: The paper expands the sequence memoizer’s hyperparameters, improves its memory representation and inference, and clarifies its mathematical foundations.

paragraphs: Resting-state fMRI can reveal groups of brain regions whose activity changes together. Correlation-based analyses identify such coherent groups, but provide less insight into interactions among them. This paper shifts attention toward groups defined by coherent relationships with other parts of the brain, making the pattern of interactions central to the analysis.

The approach measures relationships using mutual information and applies an infinite relational model to identify functionally coherent units. The organizing idea is that regions can be grouped according to how they communicate with the wider network. This produces components together with a description of their interactions, rather than focusing only on similarity within a component.

The authors demonstrate that these extracted interactions can discriminate between resting-state activity in people with multiple sclerosis and normal subjects. The finding gives the interaction-based representation a concrete use in comparing the studied groups. It supports analyzing how functional units relate to one another as an informative aspect of whole-brain resting-state organization.
neurips-2010-infinite-relational-modelin.tldr: An infinite relational model groups brain regions by their interactions and uses those interactions to distinguish studied resting-state subject groups.

paragraphs: A collection of documents contains themes and relationships that are difficult to summarize through keyword search alone. This paper learns concept graphs intended to provide a visual overview of that thematic content. The model can represent different graph structures and can incorporate partial knowledge about the graph alongside labeled documents.

The authors formulate a generative probabilistic model based on a stick-breaking process for graphs. They use Markov chain Monte Carlo for inference. Together, these provide a way to learn graph structure from text while allowing either unsupervised learning or semi-supervised learning that includes supplied information.

On simulated data, the model recovers known graph structure in both learning modes. On real text datasets, its empirical log likelihood is competitive with structure-based topic models including hPAM and hLDA. The paper also illustrates updating Wikipedia category graphs. These results support both the ability to recover structure in controlled examples and the usefulness of the model for organizing real document collections.
neurips-2010-learning-concept-graphs-fro.tldr: A probabilistic stick-breaking model learns thematic concept graphs from text and can incorporate partial graph knowledge and document labels.

paragraphs: Recognizing a shape from several small views requires more than collecting local image patches. Each patch must be interpreted in relation to where it was observed, and information from multiple views must be combined. This paper studies that problem using a visual system whose high-resolution pixels cover only a small portion of an image.

The proposed model is a Boltzmann machine with third-order connections. It learns to accumulate shape information over a sequence of fixations, combining each glimpse with its fixation location before integrating it with other glimpses of the same object. Because high-resolution coverage is limited, the system must also decide on a sequence of viewing locations.

The authors evaluate the model on one synthetic dataset and two image-classification datasets. They show that it can perform at least as well as a model trained on whole images. In these evaluations, integrating localized observations therefore supplies enough information to match whole-image learning, demonstrating the effectiveness of the model’s approach to combining glimpses.
neurips-2010-learning-to-combine-foveal-.tldr: A third-order Boltzmann machine combines location-aware visual glimpses and matches or exceeds whole-image model performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A continuous movement recording may contain a succession of basic actions, such as different kinds of strokes. Recovering those actions requires deciding where one segment ends and another begins, while recognizing repeated movement types. This paper develops a probabilistic method that models a time series as a concatenation of action segments.

Each segment is generated from one of a small number of hidden trajectories representing different movement types. The observed segment can be a noisy transformation of that trajectory and can have a different time scale. This lets the model represent repeated actions whose recorded paths or durations vary, rather than requiring every occurrence to be identical.

Because working with the model directly is intractable, the authors analyze three approximation methods. They demonstrate successful segmentation of table-tennis movements recorded through a robot arm used as a haptic input device. The result shows how recurring trajectory structure and changes between movement segments can jointly support action extraction from the demonstrated continuous recordings.
neurips-2010-movement-extraction-by-dete.tldr: A probabilistic trajectory model segments repeated actions while allowing noise and timing variation, demonstrated on recorded table-tennis movements.

paragraphs: Prior information can help a reinforcement-learning system choose a model, but that information may be wrong. This paper develops PAC-Bayesian bounds for batch reinforcement learning in finite state spaces. A central property is that the bounds remain valid regardless of whether the prior distribution correctly describes the problem.

The authors show how these bounds can guide model selection in control tasks. Prior information may concern the environment’s dynamics or the values of actions, so the framework accommodates knowledge about either how the world changes or how useful actions are. The bounds provide a basis for using that information without requiring its correctness.

The empirical results show model selection benefiting from informative priors and ignoring misleading ones, in contrast with the standard Bayesian reinforcement-learning approaches discussed in the paper. The theoretical and empirical claims serve different roles: the bounds tolerate incorrect priors, while the experiments demonstrate selective use of prior information. Together they support a way to make prior knowledge useful without depending on its reliability.
neurips-2010-pac-bayesian-model-selectio.tldr: PAC-Bayesian bounds support batch reinforcement-learning model selection with priors that may be informative or misleading.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods improve decision rules using information about how changes to the policy affect expected cost. This paper develops such results for linearly solvable Markov decision processes. Its central contribution concerns the quantity that must be estimated to construct compatible function approximators and natural policy gradients within that framework.

The authors obtain these constructions by estimating the cost-to-go function, which describes future cost from a state. The traditional formulation described in the abstract instead requires a much larger state-action advantage function. Working with cost-to-go therefore changes the estimation problem underlying the gradient calculation, taking advantage of the structure of linearly solvable processes.

The paper also develops compatible function approximators and natural policy gradients for continuous-time stochastic systems, presenting these as first results of their kind. The significance is a theoretical route to policy-gradient construction in both settings. The reduction to cost-to-go is specifically established within the linearly solvable framework, where the required structure makes that alternative possible.
neurips-2010-policy-gradients-in-linearl.tldr: Linearly solvable MDPs allow natural policy gradients to be constructed from cost-to-go estimates rather than larger state-action advantage estimates.

paragraphs: Score matching provides a training criterion for high-dimensional probability models when maximum-likelihood training is intractable. Its use for natural images had been restricted to relatively simple models because differentiating the training loss with respect to parameters was difficult. This paper addresses that computational obstacle directly.

The authors extend double backpropagation to automate the required differentiation. They also introduce a regularization term for the score-matching objective. The two changes address different difficulties: automatic differentiation makes parameter learning easier to carry out, while regularization suppresses instabilities associated with finite training samples and quantized input values.

These modifications broaden the range of problems for which score matching can be used. The paper reports results on image denoising and super-resolution, connecting the training changes to image-processing applications. Its stated contribution is a more practical and stable way to estimate image statistics with score matching, combining support for richer models with an explicit response to the instabilities that arise in the specified data conditions.
neurips-2010-regularized-estimation-of-i.tldr: Automated differentiation and a stabilizing regularizer make score matching more practical for learning image statistics.

paragraphs: The paper studies least-squares regression in a finite-dimensional space built from random features. Each feature combines basis functions from an infinite-dimensional function space using independent Gaussian coefficients. For multiresolution wavelet combinations, the resulting features are called scrambled wavelets: randomness mixes information across scales before the regression model is fitted.

The authors show that these features can approximate targets in Sobolev spaces, which describe function smoothness. For targets with smoothness greater than half the input dimension, the excess-risk bound has two competing terms. One decreases with the number of features and depends on target smoothness; the other increases with the number of features relative to the sample size. Both include a logarithmic sample-size factor.

A notable property is that these bounds do not depend on the data-generating distribution. Within the stated smoothness setting, randomization therefore supports guarantees across possible input distributions. The paper also describes an efficient implementation using lazy expansions, connecting the approximation analysis to a concrete computational approach.
neurips-2010-scrambled-objects-for-least.tldr: Random Gaussian mixtures of wavelets support least-squares regression guarantees independent of the input distribution under a stated smoothness condition.

paragraphs: Training an object detector commonly requires a marked region for every object instance. This paper instead considers mixed annotation quality: some images have full regions, others indicate only whether an object is present, and others provide a rough location. The goal is to learn a detector from these heterogeneous labels together.

The method uses a discriminative structured-output formulation in which missing full annotations are latent variables. This allows weakly labeled examples to participate in learning without treating their precise object locations as known. A second contribution is a ranking objective that makes better use of images labeled as containing no target object, improving detection average precision.

The authors evaluate the approach on the INRIA pedestrian and PASCAL VOC datasets. They report performance very close to fully supervised state-of-the-art results when a significant proportion of images are weakly supervised. This demonstrates that, in the evaluated settings, a mixture of annotation strengths can preserve much of the detection performance associated with complete annotation.
neurips-2010-simultaneous-object-detecti.tldr: A latent structured model with a ranking objective learns object detectors from mixed annotation strengths while approaching fully supervised performance.

paragraphs: Finding a small unusual network inside a larger network raises a detection problem that ordinary vector-space detection theory does not directly address. This paper develops a signal-processing perspective for graph-valued data. It focuses on unweighted, undirected graphs whose background network has known statistical properties.

The detection measure uses L1 properties of eigenvectors of the graph’s modularity matrix. An L1 norm aggregates the absolute magnitudes of an eigenvector’s entries, providing a numerical feature of the graph representation. For certain categories of randomly generated graphs, the authors observe relatively little variation in this measure, making deviations potentially informative.

The method reveals anomalous subgraphs with reasonable reliability when the anomaly is not strongly correlated with more prominent background structure. That condition matters because the observed reliability depends on how the anomaly relates to the surrounding network. Analysis of real network datasets also supports the approach. The paper thus offers both a detection framework and empirical evidence for the usefulness of this eigenvector-based signal.
neurips-2010-subgraph-detection-using-ei.tldr: Modularity-matrix eigenvector L1 norms can reveal anomalous subgraphs when stronger background structure does not closely align with the anomaly.

paragraphs: Regularization influences what a learned model prefers, but its connection to the loss and observed data can be difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a robust minimax framework in which regularization terms correspond to different distortions of the original data matrix. The interpretation applies to a large class of losses.

The framework encompasses methods including ridge regression, lasso, elastic net, fused lasso, group lasso, local coordinate coding, and multiple kernel learning. Within it, the authors formally define a sparse grouping representation and prove sufficient conditions for producing sparsity at the group level. Those conditions support designing a broad set of consistent regularization terms.

The sparse grouping representation uses class or group information differently from group lasso. The paper reports that it outperforms group lasso when group labels contain noise, and also provides generalization bounds for classification. The theoretical conditions establish when the proposed group sparsity can be generated; they are sufficient conditions, rather than a claim that all possible group-sparse methods must satisfy them.
neurips-2010-sufficient-conditions-for-g.tldr: A robust minimax interpretation links regularizers to data distortions and yields sufficient conditions for a new form of group sparsity.

paragraphs: Many image models combine hidden basis functions by adding their contributions. This paper studies a strongly nonlinear alternative that takes their maximum instead. It retains a sparse prior with independent hidden variables, allowing the authors to examine how changing the combination rule affects the image features that emerge.

A variational expectation-maximization approach provides tractable approximations for learning. The resulting algorithm handles hundreds of observed and hidden variables and can infer all model parameters, including observation noise and the degree of sparsity. This makes it possible to investigate the nonlinear model at a scale the authors describe as previously computationally challenging.

Learning from image patches produces Gabor-like basis functions, showing that such edge-related features can arise without linear superposition. The learned functions also display substantial shape diversity, including strongly elongated and circularly symmetric forms. Their shape distribution reflects properties of simple-cell receptive fields that standard linear approaches do not reproduce. The findings make the rule for combining hidden causes an important part of interpreting learned image statistics.
neurips-2010-the-maximal-causes-of-natur.tldr: A sparse image model that combines basis functions through maxima learns Gabor-like features with diverse shapes resembling simple-cell receptive-field properties.

paragraphs: The max-product algorithm produces assignments for Markov random fields, but assessing an assignment’s quality requires comparing it with the optimum. This paper studies worst-case guarantees for assignments associated with any fixed point of the algorithm. The question is how good such a result must be, even in unfavorable cases.

The authors first prove a bound that does not depend on the field’s particular graph structure or parameter values. They then show that structural information can improve the guarantee, including for bipartite graphs and grids. This gives a progression from a broadly applicable bound to stronger conclusions for specified families of models.

One concrete result guarantees at least 90 percent of the optimal value for fields whose cycles satisfy the stated disjointness condition and each contain at least 20 variables. The abstract describes those cycles as variable-disjoint. This is a conditional guarantee about fixed-point assignment quality. It illustrates how the organization and size of cycles can support a much stronger assessment of max-product’s output.
neurips-2010-worst-case-bounds-on-the-qu.tldr: Worst-case bounds characterize max-product fixed-point quality, with stronger guarantees for specific graph structures and sufficiently large disjoint cycles.
